sections.heading: Relational modeling: tables, keys, relationships
paragraphs: Relational databases store rows in tables. Each row gets a primary key — a unique, stable identifier. Relationships are expressed with foreign keys: an `orders.user_id` column pointing at `users.id` says every order belongs to a user.

Cardinality drives the shape: one-to-many is a foreign key on the 'many' side. Many-to-many needs a join table — `post_tags(post_id, tag_id)` — because neither side can hold a list of the other's keys in a single column cleanly.
Normalization means each fact lives in exactly one place. Storing the user's email on every order row means an email change must update thousands of rows — or, more realistically, quietly won't.

variants.question: Posts can have many tags, and tags apply to many posts. What's the standard relational way to model this?
options: Duplicate each post row once per tag it has
A tags column on posts holding a comma-separated string of tag names
A join table post_tags(post_id, tag_id) with foreign keys to both tables
A posts column on tags holding an array of post ids
variants.rationale: Many-to-many decomposes into two one-to-many relationships through a join table. Each row of post_tags is one fact — 'this post has this tag' — indexable, constrainable, and queryable from both directions.
optionExplanations: Duplicating post rows destroys the primary key's meaning and multiplies every future update.
Comma-separated strings can't be foreign-keyed, can't be indexed usefully, and 'find posts tagged X' becomes string parsing in SQL — the classic anti-pattern.
Correct — the join table is *the* relational answer to many-to-many.
Arrays of ids can't enforce referential integrity, and querying 'tags for post 42' means scanning arrays in every tag row.
variants.interviewTip: Schema-design interviews almost always contain a hidden many-to-many. Say 'join table' early and draw it — it's often the main thing being tested.

variants.question: In a music app, a `song` can appear on many `playlist`s, and each `playlist` holds many `song`s. A junior dev proposes adding a `playlist_ids` integer column to the `songs` table. What's the correct relational model, and what's wrong with the proposal?
options: Add both a `playlist_ids` column on `songs` and a `song_ids` column on `playlists` to cover both directions
Store the relationship as a JSON blob on `playlists` for flexibility
The proposal is fine as long as `playlist_ids` is indexed
Introduce a `playlist_songs(playlist_id, song_id)` join table; the proposed column can't be foreign-keyed or queried from the playlist side without scanning every song
variants.rationale: A many-to-many between songs and playlists resolves into a join table whose every row is one membership fact. A single scalar column on `songs` can hold only one playlist id per row, and even packing many ids into it forfeits referential integrity and any efficient 'which songs are on playlist 7' lookup.
optionExplanations: Two mirror columns duplicate the same relationship in two unsynchronized places, doubling the update surface and inviting them to disagree.
A JSON blob can't be foreign-keyed, can't enforce that referenced songs exist, and turns 'playlists containing song X' into full-table JSON parsing.
Indexing a single integer column doesn't make it hold many values, and one song belongs to many playlists — the column can't represent the relationship at all.
Correct — the join table is the canonical resolution of many-to-many, queryable and constrainable from both sides.
variants.interviewTip: When two entities each own 'many' of the other, resist any single-column shortcut. Name the join table and note it can carry its own columns (e.g. `position`, `added_at`) — that extra insight signals depth.

sections.heading: Joins: recombining what normalization split
paragraphs: Normalization splits facts into separate tables; joins put them back together at query time. `INNER JOIN` returns only rows with a match on both sides. `LEFT JOIN` returns every row from the left table, with NULLs where the right side has no match.

The choice changes the question being asked. Users INNER JOIN orders: 'users who have ordered'. Users LEFT JOIN orders: 'all users, with their orders if any' — which is what a report like 'order count per user, including zero' needs.
Aggregation composes on top: `GROUP BY` collapses row groups, `COUNT`/`SUM` summarize them, and `HAVING` filters the groups after aggregation (where `WHERE` filters rows before it).

variants.question: A 'signups vs activity' report must list ALL users with their order counts — including users with zero orders. Which query shape is right?
options: users LEFT JOIN orders ... GROUP BY users.id with COUNT(orders.id)
Two separate queries concatenated with UNION
orders LEFT JOIN users ... GROUP BY orders.id
users INNER JOIN orders ... GROUP BY users.id
variants.rationale: LEFT JOIN preserves every user; those without orders get NULL order columns, and COUNT(orders.id) counts non-NULL values — yielding 0 for them. INNER JOIN would silently drop exactly the zero-order users the report exists to find.
optionExplanations: Correct — and the detail matters: COUNT(orders.id), not COUNT(*), which would count the NULL row as 1.
A UNION of 'users with orders' and 'users without' can be forced to work but is a contorted rewrite of what LEFT JOIN says directly.
This direction preserves all *orders* (which all have users anyway) and groups by the wrong entity.
INNER JOIN excludes users with no matching order — the report's most interesting rows vanish, and nothing errors to warn you.
variants.interviewTip: 'When would you use a LEFT JOIN over an INNER JOIN?' — give the concrete report: 'all users including those with zero orders.' The COUNT(column) vs COUNT(*) NULL subtlety is a bonus point interviewers notice.

variants.question: A dashboard needs the number of published comments for every blog `article`, and articles with no comments yet must show `0`. A teammate writes `articles LEFT JOIN comments ... GROUP BY articles.id` but uses `COUNT(*)`, and complaints come in that commentless articles show `1`. What actually went wrong?
options: `LEFT JOIN` was the wrong choice; an `INNER JOIN` would have shown the correct zero counts
`COUNT(*)` counts the single NULL-filled placeholder row that `LEFT JOIN` produces for a matchless article as `1`; `COUNT(comments.id)` counts only non-NULL and yields `0`
`GROUP BY articles.id` is invalid and silently returns 1 per group
The counts are off because `HAVING` was needed instead of `GROUP BY`
variants.rationale: For an article with no comments, `LEFT JOIN` still emits one row with every `comments` column NULL. `COUNT(*)` counts rows regardless of NULLs, so it counts that placeholder as 1. `COUNT(comments.id)` counts only non-NULL values of that column, correctly returning 0.
optionExplanations: `INNER JOIN` would drop the commentless articles entirely — the dashboard would show them as missing, not as 0, which is a worse failure.
Correct — the join shape was right; the bug is `COUNT(*)` versus `COUNT(comments.id)` over the NULL placeholder row.
Grouping by the primary key of the left table is valid and standard; it isn't the cause and doesn't force a count of 1.
`HAVING` filters groups after aggregation; it wouldn't fix an inflated per-group count, and none was needed here.
variants.interviewTip: The `COUNT(*)` vs `COUNT(column)` trap is a favorite because both 'look right'. Say it out loud: over a `LEFT JOIN`, count the joined table's key column, never `*`.

sections.heading: Indexes: the speed/write tradeoff
paragraphs: Without an index, `WHERE email = ?` scans every row. An index is a sorted structure (typically a B-tree) on chosen columns that lets the database seek directly — the difference between reading a phone book and reading every page of it.

Indexes aren't free: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also maintain each index, and they consume storage. You index the columns your queries actually filter, join, and sort on — driven by evidence like `EXPLAIN` output and slow-query logs, not by decoration.

Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: an index on `(user_id, created_at)` accelerates filters on `user_id` and on `user_id + created_at`, but does nothing for a filter on `created_at` alone.

variants.question: A query filtering `WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at > ?` is slow. The table has an index on (created_at, user_id). The DBA suggests (user_id, created_at) instead. Why would column order matter?
options: (created_at, user_id) is invalid SQL and was never being used
It doesn't — column order in a composite index is purely cosmetic
With user_id first, the index groups all of one user's rows together, letting the range scan on created_at run within that narrow slice; equality columns should precede range columns
Indexes can only ever use their first column
variants.rationale: A B-tree sorts by the first column, then the second within it. Leading with the equality filter (user_id) narrows to one contiguous slice, and the range on created_at scans just that slice. Leading with the range column scatters the target user's rows across the whole date range.
optionExplanations: It's valid and may even get partially used — just poorly for this query shape.
Order is one of the most consequential choices in index design — the leftmost-prefix rule depends on it entirely.
Correct — the rule of thumb: equality columns first, then the range column.
Composite indexes serve multi-column lookups all the time; the constraint is the leftmost prefix, not first-column-only.
variants.interviewTip: 'How would you speed up this slow query?' — the professional answer starts with 'first I'd run EXPLAIN', then discusses index shape. Leading with evidence beats leading with a guess.

variants.question: A table has a composite index on `(tenant_id, status, created_at)`. Three queries run against it: (A) `WHERE tenant_id = ?`, (B) `WHERE status = ? AND created_at > ?`, (C) `WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ?`. Which query can the index NOT accelerate, and why?
options: Query C, because an index needs all three columns present to be used at all
All three are accelerated equally; column order in the index is irrelevant
Query A, because a single-column filter can never use a three-column index
Query B, because it skips the leading `tenant_id` column and the leftmost-prefix rule means the index can't be seeked without it
variants.rationale: A B-tree composite index is sorted by its leading column first. Query B filters on `status` and `created_at` but never constrains `tenant_id`, so it can't use the sorted structure to seek — the leftmost prefix is missing. A uses the prefix `(tenant_id)`, and C uses the prefix `(tenant_id, status)`, so both are served.
optionExplanations: An index does not require every column to be present; any contiguous prefix from the left suffices, so C's two-column prefix works.
Column order is decisive here — it's the entire reason B fails while A and C succeed.
Query A filters exactly the leading column, which is the shortest valid leftmost prefix — the index accelerates it well.
Correct — B omits the leading `tenant_id`, breaking the leftmost-prefix requirement, so the index can't be seeked for it.
variants.interviewTip: Reframe leftmost-prefix as 'you may drop columns from the right, never from the left.' Being able to classify several queries against one index quickly is exactly the drill interviewers run.

sections.heading: Transactions: all or nothing
paragraphs: A transaction groups statements into an atomic unit: BEGIN, statements, COMMIT — or ROLLBACK, which undoes all of them. The textbook case is a money transfer: debit one account, credit another. A crash between the two without a transaction silently destroys money.

ACID names the guarantees: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work), Durability (committed means persisted).

In Prisma this is `prisma.$transaction([...])` or the interactive `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {...})`; in Drizzle, `db.transaction(async (tx) => {...})`. Same contract: throw inside, and everything rolls back.

variants.question: An order checkout does three writes: create order, decrement inventory, record payment. The server can crash at any moment. What guarantees the database never ends up with an order whose inventory was never decremented?
options: Wrap all three in a single transaction so a crash before COMMIT rolls back every write
Add a try/catch and log any errors for manual cleanup
Use three separate databases so failures stay isolated
Run the three writes in quick succession to minimize the risk window
variants.rationale: Atomicity is precisely this guarantee: until COMMIT, none of the writes are permanent; a crash mid-way leaves the database as if nothing happened. Shrinking timing windows or logging for cleanup are mitigations — a transaction is the actual solution.
optionExplanations: Correct — atomic commit/rollback is what transactions are for.
try/catch can't catch a process crash or power loss, and 'manual cleanup' means a human reconciling corrupted money data.
Splitting across databases makes atomicity *harder* (now you need distributed transactions) — the opposite of a fix.
A smaller window is still a window; under real traffic, 'rare' inconsistency becomes 'weekly' inconsistency.
variants.interviewTip: When 'transaction' comes up, name-drop the boundary decision too: keep transactions short and never hold one open across an external API call — that's where senior candidates differentiate.

variants.question: A signup flow inserts a `user` row, then inserts a matching `wallet` row seeded with a starting balance. In production, some users exist with no wallet at all. The code already wraps both inserts in `db.transaction(async (tx) => {...})`. Which ACID property is being violated, and what's the most likely cause?
options: Durability is failing; the committed wallet rows are being lost after the fact
Atomicity is likely being defeated because the second insert runs on the outer connection instead of `tx`, so it isn't part of the transaction and its failure doesn't roll back the user insert
Isolation is the problem; another transaction is deleting the wallets concurrently
Consistency is fine and this is expected behavior for transactions
variants.rationale: Atomicity means all statements in the transaction commit or none do. If the wallet insert accidentally uses the outer `db` handle rather than the transaction's `tx` handle, it executes outside the atomic unit — so it can fail (or its enclosing scope can throw after it) while the user insert still commits, producing users without wallets.
optionExplanations: Durability concerns committed data surviving crashes; here the wallet was never committed as part of the unit, so nothing durable was lost.
Correct — using `db` instead of `tx` for the inner write silently excludes it from the atomic unit, breaking all-or-nothing.
Isolation governs visibility of concurrent in-flight work; nothing here indicates a competing transaction deleting rows.
A partial result — user without wallet — is exactly what a correctly-scoped transaction is supposed to prevent, so this is not expected.
variants.interviewTip: The subtle real-world transaction bug isn't forgetting to open one — it's writing through the wrong handle inside it. Always thread `tx` (not the outer client) into every call in the block.

sections.heading: ORMs, migrations, and the N+1 trap
paragraphs: ORMs like Prisma and Drizzle map tables to typed objects: `prisma.user.findMany({ where: ... })` instead of hand-built SQL strings. You gain type safety, autocompletion, and injection-safe parameterization; you give up some control over the exact SQL emitted.

Migrations version your schema the way git versions code: each change (add column, create table) is a replayable script, so dev, staging, and prod evolve identically. Editing production schemas by hand is how environments drift apart irreversibly.

The signature ORM performance bug is N+1: fetch 100 posts (1 query), then lazily fetch each post's author inside a loop (100 more). ORMs make the loop invisible — the fix is telling the ORM up front to include the relation (`include`/`with`), collapsing it into a join or two queries.

variants.question: A page lists 100 posts with author names. Logs show 101 queries per page load. What's happening, and what's the fix?
options: The ORM's cache is disabled; enabling it removes the repeat queries
The connection pool is misconfigured; raise the pool size
Classic N+1: one query for posts, then one per post for its author. Fix: eager-load the relation (Prisma include / Drizzle with) so it's one or two queries
The database is missing an index on posts.id
variants.rationale: 1 + 100 = the N+1 signature. Each author lookup happens lazily inside the render loop. Eager loading declares the relation need up front, letting the ORM emit a join (or one batched IN query) instead of a hundred round-trips.
optionExplanations: Caching may mask it for repeated authors, but the first cold load still storms the database — and correctness now depends on cache state.
A bigger pool lets the 101 queries run more concurrently — you've optimized the symptom's throughput, not removed the 100 extra queries.
Correct — recognize the 1+N count, name the pattern, eager-load the relation.
Each per-author query is likely already an indexed fast lookup; the cost is 100 round-trips, not 100 slow queries.
variants.interviewTip: N+1 is arguably the single most-tested ORM concept in interviews. Be able to define it in one sentence and give the fix in the next.

variants.question: An API serializes 50 `order`s, and for each order accesses `order.customer.tier` and `order.shippingAddress.country`. Query logs show 101 queries per request. A developer adds `include: { customer: true }` and the count drops to 51, not 1. What's the remaining issue and the complete fix?
options: The remaining 50 queries are caused by a missing index on `orders.id`
Dropping to 51 proves the ORM cache is now working; clearing it would restore 101
51 is already optimal; a second `include` would make it slower
Only the `customer` relation was eager-loaded, so `shippingAddress` is still lazily fetched per order (the leftover +50); add it to the same `include`/`with` so all relations load up front
variants.rationale: The original 101 was 1 + 50 (customer) + 50 (address). Eager-loading only `customer` collapses one of the two N-loops, leaving 1 + 50 = 51 from the still-lazy `shippingAddress` access. Including every accessed relation in the same query removes the remaining per-row round-trips.
optionExplanations: The per-order lookups are keyed, indexed point reads; the cost is 50 extra round-trips, not a missing index.
The drop came from eager-loading `customer`, not caching; there's no cache toggle at play here.
51 still carries a full N+1 for the address relation; it is not optimal, and adding the second `include` reduces round-trips, not increases them.
Correct — a partial eager-load fixes only the relations named; every relation touched in the loop must be included.
variants.interviewTip: Partial fixes to N+1 are a classic trap: eager-loading one relation while another stays lazy. Enumerate every relation the serializer touches and include them all in a single fetch.
